He threatened to lock her up—specifically in the File Room for a day, a month—and instructed her not to talk and to ignore noise. He told her the Korean War is over and asked if she heard Ronald's cries. Manet shoved her in the small of the back and told her to go inside, back-handed her across the jaw, and elbowed her away in a gentlemanly fashion. He marched her through the corridor and supposed she would like to go back to Earth. Veronica was the lurching girl whom Ronald sidestepped, and she turned out even less bright and less equipped with information than Ronald.

Despite this mistreatment, Veronica displayed moments of tenderness toward Manet: she crept up behind him and slithered her hands up his back and over his shoulders, caressed his face to prove she liked a bristly, masculine countenance, leaned forward to breathe warmth into his ear and worry his lobe with her teeth, and sighed her instant agreement while moving her hands over his chest and throat. She lowered her long blonde lashes on her pink cheeks, called Manet mean, and forgave him. She said "Now?" and "Oh, yes" in response to his suggestion, and "Whenever you say." She said hesitantly that if Manet thought it was the right thing, and wistfully remarked that if Manet were a jet pilot he would be romantic and grab love when he could. She honestly felt that Bill should let her out, and she made her return. Veronica snapped at Manet that if the Korean War were over she would know about it, and she said not to be silly, asking who else would stop the vile North Koreans and Red China volunteers. She also said that Daniel Boone only killed three Indians in his life. At one point she sprang forward and led with a right punch. She was still following Manet's orders to ignore the noise.

Despite this, Manet regards Ronald as a “terrific jerk,” someone he yells at to shut up, wants to change or shut off using the Modifier, and someone whose parts could be taken; yet Ronald is also a person Manet will have forever, who will never change.

Physically, Ronald appears just the same as when Manet last saw him, with a trifle chapped lips resulting from having nothing to drink for some months, though his hands show no signs of being worn away. He was shoved into the File Room by Manet on Lincoln’s Birthday and locked in the Usher tomb of the File Room, where he became trapped and called out to be let out. His voice carried sepulchrally as he asked Bill to open the hatch for him and said that William should let them out, telling Bill to open up; his cries grew louder as Manet marched Veronica through the corridor, and his voice dwindled stubbornly before cutting off. Ronald is more bright and better equipped with information than Veronica, and he sometimes said uncertainly that Manet knows best.

In his interactions with Manet, Ronald engaged in checker games that always ended in a tie, hopping up lightly to propose another game and once saying “Tie game.” He also initiated a fight with Manet, leaping forward and leading with his right. During the fight, he asked Manet if he had enough after being knocked down, blocked Manet’s right cross and drove a right to his navel, sidestepped a lurching girl, and separated from Manet before closing in again while puffing heavily. However, he was struck by Manet’s uppercut to the jaw, knocked to the floor, and pinwheeled to the floor. He looked offended at times, might have worn himself down to nothing before time was up, and would have worn his fists away hammering at the hatch long before. 29,	"VICTOR","PERSON",Victor serves as the adversary and enemy of Manet, functioning as a challenge, an obstacle, and a source of triumph for him. It is Victor's purpose and function to keep Manet from being bored, to constantly challenge him at every turn, and to remind him of his uselessness and the sterility of his purpose. Victor is the enemy Manet needs instead of a friend, whose presence makes a friend unnecessary. Although Victor does not want to kill Manet—and indeed cannot, being too human and too like Manet—he refrains also because killing Manet would leave him with nothing left to do.

Victor told Manet that he is not his friend and that Manet has made himself an enemy, speaking meanly to him, telling him to stop talking and to think about his miserable life, and warning that his friends will not grow with him and he will not make new friends. Nevertheless, Victor explained that Manet will have Veronica, Ronald, and Victor forever, and they will never change.

When Manet asked whether he had fulfilled his function, Victor answered yes, confirming that he had finished, done his worst, and destroyed the Modifier, declaring "It's finished!" and "It's done!" Victor was finished and perfect. He also smiled and asked whether Manet was going to denounce him for a fiend.

Victor is the model whose left eyelid was lifted and nose tweaked by Manet. He stepped out of the oblong box and declared that he is different from the others, and later leaped back into the Lifo kit and did a jig on one of the flesh-sprayers. When Manet made a claim, Victor stormed and cited a fundamental safety cut-off, exclaiming "Of course not! Fundamental safety cut-off!"
30,	"PETER MANNERS","PERSON",Peter Manners arrived at the Lex Industries plant fifteen minutes early for a job interview as an engineer, believing that coming early would betray overeagerness. He studied the building and found it so plain and ordinary that it was like no other building he had seen, with no windows at the side or rear. He observed a strange door configuration and, after finding the electric service lines at one of the rear corners, was jolted by the size of the transformers. He considered walking around the building to kill time and stopped to look for a photo-electric eye. He felt the room was like Hollywood's idea of an office, and as doors kept opening and shutting, he felt this was no way to go into an interview.

Peter Manners straightened his jacket and tie and walked in as an engineer should, though he went through the doors with his composure slipping. He was addressed by a soft voice through a loudspeaker and was asked if he was Mr. Manners. He said thanks, and a door swung open for him; he nodded and was told to follow the open doors down the hall. At one point he was yelled at to come in or go away and was told not to stand out there like a jackass. After leaping toward the doorway, he stopped, took deep breaths, and thought the setup was geared to unnerve him. He ran toward the door and almost fell when it opened by itself. He panted and asked who was speaking, started, opened his mouth to answer, and closed it again. He told himself to keep his nerve.

Peter Manners came out of his flinch and observed Mr. Lexington's condition, noting that Mr. Lexington was about 65 and beginning to crumble. He introduced himself to Mr. Lexington, was told to sit down by the man at the desk, and took a chair in front of the desk, letting himself be inspected. The inspection was uncomfortable, and his eyes moved to Lexington and were daunted. Mr. Lexington asked what he could do. Peter Manners had fifteen minutes until his interview, looked at his watch and gasped, and stared at the last blank wall, suddenly remembering the time. His nervousness was increased by Clay's admission. Peter Manners has cash reserves just above zero and faces eviction if unemployed. He looked around to ease the tension and looked for minutes before finding what else was wrong.

William Manet was alone.


 In the beginning, he had seen many advantages to being alone. It would
 give him an unprecedented opportunity to once and for all correlate
 loneliness to the point of madness, to see how long it would take him
 to start slavering and clawing the pin-ups from the magazines, to begin

 He would be able to measure the qualities of peace and decide whether

 dirty as he liked, he would be able to live more like an animal and
 think more like a god than any man for generations.


 But after a shorter time than he expected, it all got to be a tearing
 bore. Even the waiting to go crazy part of it.


 Not that he was going to have any great long wait of it. He was already
 talking to himself, making verbal notes for his lectures, and he had
 cut out a picture of Annie Oakley from an old book. He tacked it up and
 winked at it whenever he passed that way.


 Lately she was winking back at him.


 Loneliness was a physical weight on his skull. It peeled the flesh from
 his arms and legs and sandpapered his self-pity to a fine sensitivity.


 No one on Earth was as lonely as William Manet, and even William Manet
 could only be this lonely on Mars.


 Manet was Atmosphere Seeder Station 131-47's own human.


 All Manet had to do was sit in the beating aluminum heart in the middle
 of the chalk desert and stare out, chin cupped in hands, at the flat,
 flat pavement of dirty talcum, at the stars gleaming as hard in the
 black sky as a starlet's capped teeth ... stars two of which were moons
 and one of which was Earth. He had to do nothing else. The whole
 gimcrack was cybernetically controlled, entirely automatic. No one was
 needed here—no human being, at least.


 The Workers' Union was a pretty small pressure group, but it didn't
 take much to pressure the Assembly. Featherbedding had been carefully

 They didn't give tests to find well-balanced, well-integrated people

 isolate themselves in a useless job. They got, instead, William Manet
 and his fellows.

 to Mars was about one billion dollars. They weren't providing commuter
 service for night shifts. They weren't providing accommodations
 for couples when the law specified only one occupant. They weren't

Every lonely man tries to make friends.

 Manet just didn't know when to stop!
William Manet was alone.


 In the beginning, he had seen many advantages to being alone. It would
 give him an unprecedented opportunity to once and for all correlate
 loneliness to the point of madness, to see how long it would take him
 to start slavering and clawing the pin-ups from the magazines, to begin
 teaching himself classes in philosophy consisting of interminable
 lectures to a bored and captive audience of one.


 He would be able to measure the qualities of peace and decide whether
 it was really better than war, he would be able to get as fat and as
 dirty as he liked, he would be able to live more like an animal and
 think more like a god than any man for generations.


 But after a shorter time than he expected, it all got to be a tearing
 bore. Even the waiting to go crazy part of it.


 Not that he was going to have any great long wait of it. He was already
 talking to himself, making verbal notes for his lectures, and he had
 cut out a picture of Annie Oakley from an old book. He tacked it up and
 winked at it whenever he passed that way.


 Lately she was winking back at him.


 Loneliness was a physical weight on his skull. It peeled the flesh from
 his arms and legs and sandpapered his self-pity to a fine sensitivity.


 No one on Earth was as lonely as William Manet, and even William Manet
 could only be this lonely on Mars.


 Manet was Atmosphere Seeder Station 131-47's own human.


 All Manet had to do was sit in the beating aluminum heart in the middle
 of the chalk desert and stare out, chin cupped in hands, at the flat,
 flat pavement of dirty talcum, at the stars gleaming as hard in the
 black sky as a starlet's capped teeth ... stars two of which were moons
 and one of which was Earth. He had to do nothing else. The whole
 gimcrack was cybernetically controlled, entirely automatic. No one was
 needed here—no human being, at least.


 The Workers' Union was a pretty small pressure group, but it didn't
 take much to pressure the Assembly. Featherbedding had been carefully
 specified, including an Overseer for each of the Seeders to honeycomb

HOW TO MAKE FRIENDS
By JIM HARMON


 Illustrated by WEST


 [Transcriber's Note: This etext was produced from

 Galaxy Magazine October 1962.

 Extensive research did not uncover any evidence that

Every lonely man tries to make friends.

 Manet just didn't know when to stop!
William Manet was alone.


 In the beginning, he had seen many advantages to being alone. It would
 give him an unprecedented opportunity to once and for all correlate
 loneliness to the point of madness, to see how long it would take him
 to start slavering and clawing the pin-ups from the magazines, to begin
 teaching himself classes in philosophy consisting of interminable
 lectures to a bored and captive audience of one.


 He would be able to measure the qualities of peace and decide whether
 it was really better than war, he would be able to get as fat and as
 dirty as he liked, he would be able to live more like an animal and
 think more like a god than any man for generations.


 But after a shorter time than he expected, it all got to be a tearing
 bore. Even the waiting to go crazy part of it.


 Not that he was going to have any great long wait of it. He was already
 talking to himself, making verbal notes for his lectures, and he had
 cut out a picture of Annie Oakley from an old book. He tacked it up and
 winked at it whenever he passed that way.


 Lately she was winking back at him.


 Loneliness was a physical weight on his skull. It peeled the flesh from
 his arms and legs and sandpapered his self-pity to a fine sensitivity.


 No one on Earth was as lonely as William Manet, and even William Manet
 could only be this lonely on Mars.


 Manet was Atmosphere Seeder Station 131-47's own human.


 All Manet had to do was sit in the beating aluminum heart in the middle
 of the chalk desert and stare out, chin cupped in hands, at the flat,
 flat pavement of dirty talcum, at the stars gleaming as hard in the
 black sky as a starlet's capped teeth ... stars two of which were moons
 and one of which was Earth. He had to do nothing else. The whole
 gimcrack was cybernetically controlled, entirely automatic. No one was
 needed here—no human being, at least.


 The Workers' Union was a pretty small pressure group, but it didn't
 take much to pressure the Assembly. Featherbedding had been carefully
 specified, including an Overseer for each of the Seeders to honeycomb
 Mars, to prepare its atmosphere for colonization.


 They didn't give tests to find well-balanced, well-integrated people
 for the job. Well-balanced, well-integrated men weren't going to
 isolate themselves in a useless job. They got, instead, William Manet
 and his fellows.


 The Overseers were to stay as long as the job required. Passenger fare
 to Mars was about one billion dollars. They weren't providing commuter
 service for night shifts. They weren't providing accommodations
 for couples when the law specified only one occupant. They weren't
 providing fuel (at fifty million dollars a gallon) for visits between
 the various Overseers. They weren't very providential.


 But it was two hundred thousand a year in salary, and it offered
 wonderful opportunities.


 It gave William Manet an opportunity to think he saw a spaceship making
 a tailfirst landing on the table of the desert, its tail burning as
 bright as envy.
Manet suspected hallucination, but in an existence with all the pallid
 dispassion of a requited love he was happy to welcome dementia.
 Sometimes he even manufactured it. Sometimes he would run through the
 arteries of the factory and play that it had suddenly gone mad hating
 human beings, and was about to close down its bulkheads on him as sure
 as the Engineers' Thumb and bale up the pressure-dehydrated digest,
 making so much stall flooring of him. He ran until he dropped with a
 kind of climaxing release of terror.


 So Manet put on the pressure suit he had been given because he would
 never need it, and marched out to meet the visiting spaceship.


 He wasn't quite clear how he came from walking effortlessly across
 the Martian plain that had all the distance-perpetuating qualities of
 a kid's crank movie machine to the comfortable interior of a strange
 cabin. Not a ship's cabin but a Northwoods cabin.


 The black and orange Hallowe'en log charring in the slate stone
 fireplace seemed real. So did the lean man with the smiling mustache
 painted with the random designs of the fire, standing before the
 horizontal pattern of chinked wall.


 "Need a fresher?" the host inquired.


 Manet's eyes wondered down to heavy water tumbler full of rich, amber
 whiskey full of sparks from the hearth. He stirred himself in the
 comfortingly warm leather chair. "No, no, I'm
fine
." He let the word
 hang there for examination. "Pardon me, but could you tell me just what
 place this is?"


 The host shrugged. It was the only word for it. "Whatever place you
 choose it to be, so long as you're with Trader Tom. 'Service,' that's
 my motto. It is a way of life with me."


 "Trader Tom? Service?"


 "Yes! That's it exactly. It's

He is a person into whose mind pictures and waves of thought enter with plain meaning, indicating telepathic abilities common to his people.

Ro’s story is marked by both personal loss and heroic action. He returns from a journey to the north, where he saw great villages of thatched huts and strange people, only to find his homecoming overshadowed by tragedy. His father, brothers, and tribe have been killed, and he is determined to avenge them with the help of white people—strangers from Earth who have arrived on Mars. Ro rescues these white people from the Oan, a race of rat-like beings, and allies with them to fight the Oan and free captives. He is courageous and resourceful, planning ambushes, using his knowledge of the terrain, and even risking his life to save others. Ro is also a person who arose from his crouch like a phantom and killed an Oan guard with a stone, and who later fought a rat man to save Na, the woman he has chosen as his mate.

Ro’s relationship with Na is central to his story. He declares Na as his mate according to the custom of his tribe, which involves a kiss and a promise, and he is protective of her, though he respects her independence. He is puzzled by Earth customs, particularly the concept of “year” and marriage, and questions the white people about their world. Ro is eager to learn more about them and their weapons, believing they will help him make more weapons to defeat the Oan. Despite his stern demeanor, Ro is capable of tenderness, as seen when he gathers Na in his arms, speaks softly to her, and sleeps with their heads together.

22,	"VERONICA","PERSON",Veronica is a complex figure whose interactions with Manet reveal a deeply troubled and abusive relationship. She is described as a person Manet will have forever and who will never change. Veronica was behind a locked door with Manet's best friend, and Manet accused her of being cloyingly sweet and having no fight. Manet called her stupidity hideous and stated that her parts could be taken by him. He threatened to lock her up—specifically in the File Room for a day, a month—and instructed her not to talk and to ignore noise. He told her the Korean War is over and asked if she heard Ronald's cries. Manet shoved her in the small of the back and told her to go inside, back-handed her across the jaw, and elbowed her away in a gentlemanly fashion. He marched her through the corridor and supposed she would like to go back to Earth. Veronica was the lurching girl whom Ronald sidestepped, and she turned out even less bright and less equipped with information than Ronald.

Despite this mistreatment, Veronica displayed moments of tenderness toward Manet: she crept up behind him and slithered her hands up his back and over his shoulders, caressed his face to prove she liked a bristly, masculine countenance, leaned forward to breathe warmth into his ear and worry his lobe with her teeth, and sighed her instant agreement while moving her hands over his chest and throat. She lowered her long blonde lashes on her pink cheeks, called Manet mean, and forgave him. She said "Now?" and "Oh, yes" in response to his suggestion, and "Whenever you say." She said hesitantly that if Manet thought it was the right thing, and wistfully remarked that if Manet were a jet pilot he would be romantic and grab love when he could. She honestly felt that Bill should let her out, and she made her return. Veronica snapped at Manet that if the Korean War were over she would know about it, and she said not to be silly, asking who else would stop the vile North Koreans and Red China volunteers. She also said that Daniel Boone only killed three Indians in his life. At one point she sprang forward and led with a right punch. She was still following Manet's orders to ignore the noise.

A skilled and cautious traveler, Ro is aware of the dangers of his world and moves with stealth and precision, capable of surviving in the wild and navigating the almost smooth walls of cliffs on dark nights. He is a person into whose mind pictures and waves of thought enter with plain meaning, indicating telepathic abilities common to his people.

Ro’s story is marked by both personal loss and heroic action. He returns from a journey to the north, where he saw great villages of thatched huts and strange people, only to find his homecoming overshadowed by tragedy. His father, brothers, and tribe have been killed, and he is determined to avenge them with the help of white people—strangers from Earth who have arrived on Mars. Ro rescues these white people from the Oan, a race of rat-like beings, and allies with them to fight the Oan and free captives. He is courageous and resourceful, planning ambushes, using his knowledge of the terrain, and even risking his life to save others. Ro is also a person who arose from his crouch like a phantom and killed an Oan guard with a stone, and who later fought a rat man to save Na, the woman he has chosen as his mate.

Ro’s relationship with Na is central to his story. Ro is eager to learn more about them and their weapons, believing they will help him make more weapons to defeat the Oan. Despite his stern demeanor, Ro is capable of tenderness, as seen when he gathers Na in his arms, speaks softly to her, and sleeps with their heads together.

26,	"CARLSON","PERSON",Carlson is a lean, determined young Earthman with black hair and white skin, and one of the old man's two assistants. He is romantically involved with Charlotte, whom he slept beside, and the two plan to marry upon returning to America. Carlson is often associated with Ro, with whom he shared a silent climb up the sloping part of the mountain after coming out of a trance, and together they reached the top and piled rocks and boulders at the edge of the cliff. He is capable of joining Ro, or the speaker, in rolling an avalanche of rocks down on their enemies and asked how the six of them would attack the rat men.

Carlson has a complicated relationship with Ro: he charged at Grimm but was caught and forced back by Ro, and was once asked by Ro whether fear of Grimm prevented a more tender goodbye with Charlotte. Carlson was also hit in the shoulder by a rock thrown by Grimm. When questioned about being saved for the professor's daughter—a suggestion made by Grimm and later by Ro, who proposed Carlson take Charlotte as his wife on Mars—Carlson straightened, weighed Ro's words, said he didn't want to make trouble, and revealed his marriage plans with Charlotte. He also grabbed Grimm by the shoulder, spun him around, and drove a hard fist into his face.

Carlson is assigned to accompany the professor, and he agreed to go with Ro when asked. On matters of marriage, he laughed and argued the point about Hollywood, noting that marriage and divorce there is bad enough, that under Ro's system it would really be a mess, and that on Mars a kiss and a promise is probably as binding as any ceremony; he also seemed surprised that a wedding there wouldn't be legal and asked who would perform the ceremony. Carlson can communicate with Ro through pictures, though these were confusing, and like the young Earthman, he was observed looking at Charlotte in much the same way.
27,	"GRIMM","PERSON",GRIMM is one of the old man's two assistants, described as a stouter, less impressive man with black hair and white skin who acknowledged the introduction. At the cave's entrance, Grimm climbed to his feet, brushed himself off, and backed away from Ro, who accused him of lying and being a coward. Carlson then charged at Grimm, grabbed him by the shoulder, spun him around, and punched him in the face. Grimm stumbled backward, fell at the cave's entrance, grabbed a rock, and flung it at Carlson from a sitting position.

Following this, Grimm agreed to go with the red man (or with Ro), though he threatened a different story when they meet again. He demanded to know why he was chosen instead of Carlson, questioning whether Carlson was being saved for the professor's daughter. Carlson, who might fear Grimm, is nevertheless sure Grimm will see reason when they tell him, and Grimm is no longer in the running for Charlotte. Grimm also laughed and remarked that it takes intricate machinery to construct a ray gun, and that they only have sticks and stones in the wilderness. He stated aloud that the professor should tell Ro that he is speaking the truth.

In terms of group assignments, Grimm can go with one group, including Charlotte and the professor, or with the speaker/you, and he is also assigned to go with Ro. Additionally, Grimm can be with Ro or the speaker to roll an avalanche of rocks on their heads.

37,	"RO","PERSON",Ro is a young Martian man, deeply familiar with the jungles and cliffs of Mars, having lived among them all his life. He is physically striking, with bare head and back, red skin that glistens, thick black hair that shines healthily under the sun, and long, well-muscled legs that carry him swiftly and gracefully. A skilled and cautious traveler, Ro is aware of the dangers of his world and moves with stealth and precision, capable of surviving in the wild and navigating the almost smooth walls of cliffs on dark nights. He is a person into whose mind pictures and waves of thought enter with plain meaning, indicating telepathic abilities common to his people.

Ro’s story is marked by both personal loss and heroic action. He returns from a journey to the north, where he saw great villages of thatched huts and strange people, only to find his homecoming overshadowed by tragedy. His father, brothers, and tribe have been killed, and he is determined to avenge them with the help of white people—strangers from Earth who have arrived on Mars. Ro rescues these white people from the Oan, a race of rat-like beings, and allies with them to fight the Oan and free captives. He is courageous and resourceful, planning ambushes, using his knowledge of the terrain, and even risking his life to save others. Ro is also a person who arose from his crouch like a phantom and killed an Oan guard with a stone, and who later fought a rat man to save Na, the woman he has chosen as his mate.

Ro’s relationship with Na is central to his story. He declares Na as his mate according to the custom of his tribe, which involves a kiss and a promise, and he is protective of her, though he respects her independence. He is puzzled by Earth customs, particularly the concept of “year” and marriage, and questions the white people about their world. Ro is eager to learn more about them and their weapons, believing they will help him make more weapons to defeat the Oan. Despite his stern demeanor, Ro is capable of tenderness, as seen when he gathers Na in his arms, speaks softly to her, and sleeps with their heads together.

By W. T. HAGGERT

Nothing in the world could be happier and
 
mere serene than a man who loves his work—but
 
what happens when it loves him back?
Keep your nerve, Peter Manners told himself; it's only a job. But nerve
 has to rest on a sturdier foundation than cash reserves just above zero
 and eviction if he came away from this interview still unemployed.
 Clay, at the Association of Professional Engineers, who had set up the
 appointment, hadn't eased Peter's nervousness by admitting, "I don't
 know what in hell he's looking for. He's turned down every man we've
 sent him."


 The interview was at three. Fifteen minutes to go. Coming early would
 betray overeagerness. Peter stood in front of the Lex Industries plant
 and studied it to kill time. Plain, featureless concrete walls, not
 large for a manufacturing plant—it took a scant minute to exhaust its
 sightseeing potential. If he walked around the building, he could, if
 he ambled, come back to the front entrance just before three.


 He turned the corner, stopped, frowned, wondering what there was about
 the building that seemed so puzzling. It could not have been plainer,
 more ordinary. It was in fact, he only gradually realized, so plain and
 ordinary that it was like no other building he had ever seen.


 There had been windows at the front. There were none at the side, and
 none at the rear. Then how were the working areas lit? He looked for
 the electric service lines and found them at one of the rear corners.
 They jolted him. The distribution transformers were ten times as large
 as they should have been for a plant this size.


 Something else was wrong. Peter looked for minutes before he found out
 what it was. Factories usually have large side doorways for employees
 changing shifts. This building had one small office entrance facing the
 street, and the only other door was at the loading bay—big enough to
 handle employee traffic, but four feet above the ground. Without any
 stairs, it could be used only by trucks backing up to it. Maybe the
 employees' entrance was on the third side.


 It wasn't.
Staring back at the last blank wall, Peter suddenly remembered the time
 he had set out to kill. He looked at his watch and gasped. At a run,
 set to straight-arm the door, he almost fell on his face. The door had
 opened by itself. He stopped and looked for a photo-electric eye, but
 a soft voice said through a loudspeaker in the anteroom wall: "Mr.
 Manners?"


 "What?" he panted. "Who—?"


 "You
are

By W. T. HAGGERT

 [Transcriber's Note: This etext was produced from

Nothing in the world could be happier and
 
mere serene than a man who loves his work—but
 
what happens when it loves him back?
Keep your nerve, Peter Manners told himself; it's only a job. But nerve
 has to rest on a sturdier foundation than cash reserves just above zero
 and eviction if he came away from this interview still unemployed.
 Clay, at the Association of Professional Engineers, who had set up the
 appointment, hadn't eased Peter's nervousness by admitting, "I don't
 know what in hell he's looking for. He's turned down every man we've
 sent him."


 The interview was at three. Fifteen minutes to go. Coming early would
 betray overeagerness. Peter stood in front of the Lex Industries plant
 and studied it to kill time. Plain, featureless concrete walls, not
 large for a manufacturing plant—it took a scant minute to exhaust its
 sightseeing potential. If he walked around the building, he could, if
 he ambled, come back to the front entrance just before three.


 He turned the corner, stopped, frowned, wondering what there was about
 the building that seemed so puzzling. It could not have been plainer,
 more ordinary. It was in fact, he only gradually realized, so plain and
 ordinary that it was like no other building he had ever seen.


 There had been windows at the front. There were none at the side, and
 none at the rear. Then how were the working areas lit? He looked for
 the electric service lines and found them at one of the rear corners.
 They jolted him. The distribution transformers were ten times as large
 as they should have been for a plant this size.


 Something else was wrong. Peter looked for minutes before he found out
 what it was. Factories usually have large side doorways for employees
 changing shifts. This building had one small office entrance facing the
 street, and the only other door was at the loading bay—big enough to
 handle employee traffic, but four feet above the ground. Without any
 stairs, it could be used only by trucks backing up to it. Maybe the
 employees' entrance was on the third side.


 It wasn't.
Staring back at the last blank wall, Peter suddenly remembered the time
 he had set out to kill. He looked at his watch and gasped. At a run,
 set to straight-arm the door, he almost fell on his face. The door had
 opened by itself. He stopped and looked for a photo-electric eye, but
 a soft voice said through a loudspeaker in the anteroom wall: "Mr.
 Manners?"


 "What?" he panted. "Who—?"


 "You
are
Mr. Manners?" the voice asked.


 He nodded, then realized he had to answer aloud if there was a
 microphone around; but the soft voice said: "Follow the open doors down
 the hall. Mr. Lexington is expecting you."


 "Thanks," Peter said, and a door at one side of the anteroom swung open
 for him.


 He went through it with his composure slipping still further from his
 grip. This was no way to go into an interview, but doors kept opening
 before and shutting after him, until only one was left, and the last of
 his calm was blasted away by a bellow from within.


 "Don't stand out there like a jackass! Either come in or go away!"


 Peter found himself leaping obediently toward the doorway. He stopped
 just short of it, took a deep breath and huffed it out, took another,
 all the while thinking, Hold on now; you're in no shape for an
 interview—and it's not your fault—this whole setup is geared to
 unnerve you: the kindergarten kid called in to see the principal.


 He let another bellow bounce off him as he blew out the second breath,
 straightened his jacket and tie, and walked in as an engineer applying
 for a position should.


 "Mr. Lexington?" he said. "I'm Peter Manners. The Association—"


 "Sit down," said the man at the desk. "Let's look you over."


 He was a huge man behind an even huger desk. Peter took a chair in
 front of the desk and let himself be inspected. It wasn't comfortable.
 He did some looking over of his own to ease the tension.


 The room was more than merely large, carpeted throughout with
 a high-pile, rich, sound-deadening rug. The oversized desk and
 massive leather chairs, heavy patterned drapes, ornately framed

 complexion ashen, the eyes set deep as though retreating from pain, and

Nothing in the world could be happier and

Keep your nerve, Peter Manners told himself; it's only a job. But nerve
 has to rest on a sturdier foundation than cash reserves just above zero
 and eviction if he came away from this interview still unemployed.
 Clay, at the Association of Professional Engineers, who had set up the
 appointment, hadn't eased Peter's nervousness by admitting, "I don't
 know what in hell he's looking for. He's turned down every man we've
 sent him."


 The interview was at three. Fifteen minutes to go. Coming early would
 betray overeagerness. Peter stood in front of the Lex Industries plant
 and studied it to kill time. Plain, featureless concrete walls, not
 large for a manufacturing plant—it took a scant minute to exhaust its
 sightseeing potential. If he walked around the building, he could, if
 he ambled, come back to the front entrance just before three.


 He turned the corner, stopped, frowned, wondering what there was about
 the building that seemed so puzzling. It could not have been plainer,
 more ordinary. It was in fact, he only gradually realized, so plain and
 ordinary that it was like no other building he had ever seen.


 There had been windows at the front. There were none at the side, and
 none at the rear. Then how were the working areas lit? He looked for
 the electric service lines and found them at one of the rear corners.
 They jolted him. The distribution transformers were ten times as large
 as they should have been for a plant this size.


 Something else was wrong. Peter looked for minutes before he found out
 what it was. Factories usually have large side doorways for employees
 changing shifts. This building had one small office entrance facing the
 street, and the only other door was at the loading bay—big enough to
 handle employee traffic, but four feet above the ground. Without any
 stairs, it could be used only by trucks backing up to it. Maybe the

Nothing in the world could be happier and

what happens when it loves him back?
Keep your nerve, Peter Manners told himself; it's only a job. But nerve
 has to rest on a sturdier foundation than cash reserves just above zero
 and eviction if he came away from this interview still unemployed.
 Clay, at the Association of Professional Engineers, who had set up the
 appointment, hadn't eased Peter's nervousness by admitting, "I don't
 know what in hell he's looking for. He's turned down every man we've
 sent him."


 The interview was at three. Fifteen minutes to go. Coming early would
 betray overeagerness. Peter stood in front of the Lex Industries plant
 and studied it to kill time. Plain, featureless concrete walls, not
 large for a manufacturing plant—it took a scant minute to exhaust its
 sightseeing potential. If he walked around the building, he could, if
 he ambled, come back to the front entrance just before three.


 He turned the corner, stopped, frowned, wondering what there was about
 the building that seemed so puzzling. It could not have been plainer,
 more ordinary. It was in fact, he only gradually realized, so plain and
 ordinary that it was like no other building he had ever seen.


 There had been windows at the front. There were none at the side, and
 none at the rear. Then how were the working areas lit? He looked for
 the electric service lines and found them at one of the rear corners.
 They jolted him. The distribution transformers were ten times as large
 as they should have been for a plant this size.


 Something else was wrong. Peter looked for minutes before he found out
 what it was. Factories usually have large side doorways for employees
 changing shifts. This building had one small office entrance facing the
 street, and the only other door was at the loading bay—big enough to
 handle employee traffic, but four feet above the ground. Without any
 stairs, it could be used only by trucks backing up to it. Maybe the
 employees' entrance was on the third side.


 It wasn't.
Staring back at the last blank wall, Peter suddenly remembered the time
 he had set out to kill. He looked at his watch and gasped. At a run,
 set to straight-arm the door, he almost fell on his face. The door had
 opened by itself. He stopped and looked for a photo-electric eye, but
 a soft voice said through a loudspeaker in the anteroom wall: "Mr.
 Manners?"


 "What?" he panted. "Who—?"

are
Mr. Manners?" the voice asked.


 He nodded, then realized he had to answer aloud if there was a
 microphone around; but the soft voice said: "Follow the open doors down
 the hall. Mr. Lexington is expecting you."


 "Thanks," Peter said, and a door at one side of the anteroom swung open
 for him.


 He went through it with his composure slipping still further from his
 grip. This was no way to go into an interview, but doors kept opening
 before and shutting after him, until only one was left, and the last of
 his calm was blasted away by a bellow from within.


 "Don't stand out there like a jackass! Either come in or go away!"


 Peter found himself leaping obediently toward the doorway. He stopped
 just short of it, took a deep breath and huffed it out, took another,
 all the while thinking, Hold on now; you're in no shape for an
 interview—and it's not your fault—this whole setup is geared to

 He let another bellow bounce off him as he blew out the second breath,
